content: Pantethine, also known as bis-pantethine or co-enzyme pantethine, is a dimeric compound derived from pantothenic acid (vitamin B5). It consists of two pantothenic acid molecules connected by cysteamine bridging groups. The monomeric form of this compound is called pantetheine, which serves as an intermediate in the biosynthesis of Coenzyme A within the body. Pantethine is regarded as the biologically active form of vitamin B5, but it is inherently less stable and tends to degrade over time unless stored under refrigeration. For this reason, most vitamin B5 supplements are formulated as calcium pantothenate, a more stable salt form of pantothenic acid. Pantethine is available as a dietary supplement due to its demonstrated health benefits. Clinical trials involving individuals with elevated cholesterol and triglyceride levels have shown that pantethine supplementation can reduce total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol by approximately 12%, lower triglycerides by 18%, and increase HDL cholesterol by 9%. These effects were observed with daily doses ranging from 600 to 1200 mg. Within this dosage range, no clear dose-response relationship has been identified, as the changes in lipid profiles were similar across the tested doses. Notably, no clinical trial has directly compared multiple doses within a single study. However, a few studies using a lower dose of 300 mg/day reported more modest but still statistically significant improvements in lipid parameters. The physiological effects of pantethine are not attributed to its role as a precursor for vitamin B5 synthesis, as the daily requirement for vitamin B5 is only about 5 mg, whereas effective pantethine doses range from 600 to 1200 mg/day. Furthermore, high doses of vitamin B5 alone do not produce the same lipid-lowering effects as pantethine. Two primary mechanisms of action have been proposed for pantethine. First, it may act as a precursor for the synthesis of Coenzyme A, a critical cofactor in numerous metabolic pathways. Second, pantethine may be metabolized into two pantetheine molecules, which are further broken down into pantothenic acid and cysteamine. Cysteamine is hypothesized to bind to and inactivate sulfur-containing amino acids in hepatic enzymes that are involved in the synthesis of cholesterol and triglycerides, thereby reducing their production.
